Orthodox thought but greatly influence Orthodox thinkers today.

slides.text:
Council of Basel/Florence (1431–1449)
Primary Objective: Continue the reform agenda outlined at Constance and negotiate reunion with the Eastern Orthodox Church.
The Conciliarist Peak: At Basel, the council operated independently of the Pope, attempting to severely limit papal taxation, abolish annates, and curb the Roman Curia's administrative power.
The Split & Failure: Pope Eugene IV attempted to dissolve the council and moved his faction to Ferrara (and later Florence). The remaining radical conciliarists at Basel elected an antipope (Felix V), which alienated European monarchs. The conciliar movement collapsed, allowing the papacy to reassert absolute monarchical control.
slides.title: Council of Basel/Florence (1431–1449)

slides.text:
Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517)
Primary Objective: Initiated by Pope Julius II (and concluded under Pope Leo X) as a direct papal counter-measure against a rival, French-backed council in Pisa (the Conciliabulum of Pisa, 1511).
Reform Decrees: Promulgated decrees on paper calling for:
Restrictions on clerical absenteeism and pluralism
Reforms in preaching standards and censorship of printed books.
Structural administrative limits on cardinal revenues.
Why It Failed: The decrees lacked enforcement mechanisms and papal will. The council officially closed on March 16, 1517 (just seven months before Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in Wittenberg) marking the final failed effort at top-down, pre-Reformation Catholic self-reform.
slides.title: Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517)

MARIAN DOGMAS
This new interest in grace and justification led to a new concern with
understanding the role of Mary, the mother of Jesus Christ, in salvation. Growing
interest in devotion to Mary, linked with intense theological speculation
concerning the nature of original sin and redemption, led to a series of
developments relating to Mary.
Intense debate broke out between "maculists" (who held that Mary was subject to
original sin, like everyone else) and "immaculists" (who held that she was
preserved from the taint of original sin). There was also considerable discussion
over whether Mary could be said to be coredemptrix (that is to say, whether she
was to be regarded as a figure of redemption, in a manner similar to Jesus Christ).”
slides.title: MARIAN DOGMAS

slides.text:
MARIAN DOGMAS
Erasmus showed that the Vulgate translation of several major New Testament texts could not
be justified - with important theological implica-tions. Two examples of translation errors will
help to bring out the theological relevance of Erasmus's biblical scholarship.
1 The Vulgate translated the opening words of Jesus's ministry (Matthew 4: 17) as "do
pen-ance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." This translation suggested that the coming of
the kingdom of heaven had a direct connection with the sacrament of penance. Erasmus
pointed out that the original Greek text should be translated as "repent, for the kingdom of
heaven is at hand." In other words, where the Vulgate seemed to refer to an outward practice
(the sacrament of penance), Erasmus insisted that the reference was to an inward
psychological attitude - that of "being repentant." Once more, an important justification of the
sacramental system of the medieval church was challenged.
2. According to the Vulgate translation of Luke 1:28, the angel Gabriel greeted Mary as one
who is "full of grace" (Latin: gratia plena), thus suggesting the image of a reservoir full of
grace, which could be drawn upon at time of simply meant "favored one," or "one who has
found favor." Mary was one who had found God's favor, not necessarily one who could bestow
it on others. The biblical basis of an important development within medieval theology thus
seemed to be called into question by humanist New Testament scholarship.
slides.title: MARIAN DOGMAS

slides.text:
COUNCIL OF TRENT
The final doctrinal decrees of the Council of Trent reaffirmed traditional
Catholic teachings in opposition to Protestant beliefs. Scripture and tradition
were affirmed as equal authorities in religious matters; only the church
could interpret Scripture. Both faith and good works were declared
necessary for salvation. The seven sacraments, the Catholic doctrine of
transubstantiation, and clerical celibacy were all upheld. Belief in purgatory
and in the efficacy of indulgences was affirmed, although the hawking of
indulgences was prohibited. Of the reforming decrees that were passed, the
most important established theological seminaries in every diocese for the
training of priests.
slides.title: COUNCIL OF TRENT
